topStories.headline: Wasatch County Sheriff Indicted on Felony Obstruction Charge, Will Stay in Office Through January
topStories.dek: A grand jury charged Sheriff Jared Rigby with a second-degree felony tied to alleged interference in the Kouri Richins murder prosecution; he and his co-defendant pleaded not guilty Oct. 7.
topStories.body:
A Utah grand jury has indicted Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby on a second-degree felony count of obstruction of justice and a class B misdemeanor count of making a written false statement, following an investigation into alleged interference with the prosecution of Kouri Richins, who was convicted of poisoning her husband. The charges were unsealed Wednesday, Oct. 7, in Summit County's 3rd District Court — the same courtroom where Richins was sentenced in May to life in prison without parole. Former Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds was indicted separately on a third-degree felony count of obstruction of justice. Both men pleaded not guilty.

At the center of the investigation is an anonymous letter that prosecutors in the Richins case received weeks before trial. According to a motion filed by Rigby's attorney, the charges accuse Rigby of sending the anonymous letter, which allegedly contained false information about Eric Mainord, the lead detective on the murder case — who had also filed to run against Rigby in the Republican primary for Wasatch County sheriff. Prosecutors say Rigby sought to discredit Mainord, who later dropped out of the race.

Despite the criminal charges, Rigby is expected to remain in office until January 2027, when his successor takes over. Rigby lost his reelection bid in the June primary to Jeremy Hales, who won more than 66 percent of the vote. Wasatch County Manager Dustin Grabau said the day after the indictment that the county is committed to continuity of public safety services and is reviewing state law with attorneys. Grabau indicated there may be some changes to how the sheriff fulfills his responsibilities, but normal law enforcement operations are continuing.

A hearing on whether the still-redacted portions of the indictments should be made public is scheduled for Nov. 4 before 3rd District Judge Richard Mrazik. An indictment is a formal accusation and is not a finding of guilt; prosecutors must prove the charges beyond a reasonable doubt.

topStories.headline: UDOT Pushes Heber Valley Bypass Final Environmental Review to Spring 2027
topStories.dek: The county manager previewed the delayed timeline at the Oct. 7 Wasatch County Council meeting, citing design changes under evaluation after more than 700 public comments on the preferred route.
topStories.body:
The Utah Department of Transportation now expects to finalize its environmental impact statement on the proposed Heber Valley bypass road next spring, County Manager Dustin Grabau told the Wasatch County Council in a preview of the Oct. 7 meeting, according to KPCW. The delay pushes back a project that had been expected to reach its record of decision by the end of 2026.

UDOT announced in January that it had identified Alternative B — a highway-style corridor running through the North Fields between Potters Lane and 900 North, west of Heber City — as its preferred route for the approximately $760 million project. The bypass is intended to keep through traffic on U.S. 40 off Heber City's Main Street, which UDOT projects could see backups of more than 17,000 feet by 2050 if nothing is built. More than 700 residents submitted comments during the 60-day public review period.

In July, UDOT formally announced a delay to complete supplemental wetlands and cultural-resource surveys, update traffic analysis, and evaluate potential refinements to the alignment. Heber City and Wasatch County officials had urged UDOT to shift portions of Alternative B farther east to reduce impacts on agricultural land and the North Fields irrigation system that recharges the valley's aquifer. UDOT is also reconsidering the pedestrian crossing interchange near Deer Creek High School and a raised highway connection near 1300 South.

Grabau also noted at the Oct. 7 meeting that the county may update its 2019 Heber City Expansion Area Memorandum of Understanding to include additional funding sources to preserve open space, wetlands, and aquifer recharge areas — a step that could help shape whatever alignment UDOT ultimately selects.

topStories.headline: November Ballot Takes Shape: Four Candidates Vie for Wasatch County Council Seat A as Write-Ins Join the Race
topStories.dek: With the Nov. 3 general election three weeks out, Wasatch County voters face contested races for three council seats, sheriff, county attorney, and Utah House District 59 — and a candidate forum is set for Oct. 15.
topStories.body:
Wasatch County voters will decide a crowded slate of races on Nov. 3, headlined by four candidates competing for the at-large County Council Seat A. Republican Rachel Kahler, who won the June primary, faces Democrat Robert McNeill — a former actor and television director who stepped in after the original Democratic candidate withdrew — and write-in candidates Jami Hewlett and Shawn Taylor. Taylor, a Charleston resident, entered the race after live-streaming local meetings and citing frustration with what he called a lack of transparency in government. The Park Record published profiles of both McNeill and Taylor this week.

Seat C, covering northern Heber City, pits incumbent Republican Erik Rowland against write-in candidate Alex Folmer. Seat F, covering Hideout, Timber Lakes, and rural eastern Wasatch County, is a two-way race between Republican interim councilmember Mike Murphy and Democratic challenger Joe Tugaw. The race for sheriff features Republican Jeremy Hales against write-in candidate Paul Moore. Democrat Lauren Forsyth and Republican Jon Woodard are on the ballot for county attorney, and Democrat Celeste Johnson faces Republican Luke Searle for Utah House District 59.

Residents who want to hear from the candidates before voting can attend a public Candidate Forum organized by the Heber Leadership Academy on Thursday, Oct. 15, from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Wasatch Fire District Community Room, 251 East 1200 South in Heber City. Candidates for Utah House District 59 and Council Seats A, C, and F have been invited to participate. The event is being held in partnership with KPCW and will also be available via the station's live stream. Ballots are scheduled to be mailed Oct. 13.

moreNews.headline: Midway Officially Becomes a Two-Stoplight Town
moreNews.body: UDOT activated a new four-way traffic signal at the intersection of Main Street (SR-113) and River Road (400 East) in Midway in late September 2026, nearly a decade after the intersection was first identified as a candidate for a signal. The project added dedicated turn lanes, pedestrian crossings, and bike lanes. Restoration work around the site is expected to continue through approximately Oct. 15, according to UDOT.

moreNews.headline: Hunter Airlifted After Accidental Shooting at Soapstone Basin
moreNews.body: Wasatch County Search and Rescue responded to Soapstone Basin on Saturday, Oct. 3, after a 28-year-old man was accidentally shot by his father-in-law while the two were hunting. The victim was alert when rescuers arrived, with other hunters in the area providing initial assistance. He was stabilized and flown to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries by a University of Utah AirMed helicopter. Utah recreation officials used the incident to remind hunters to practice firearm safety, particularly when putting guns away.

moreNews.headline: Wasatch County Students Outperform State Averages in 2025–26 Assessments
moreNews.body: Statewide assessment results for the 2025–26 school year, released in September, show Wasatch School District students outperforming state averages in all three core subjects: over 59% were proficient in English, nearly 57% in math, and 61% in science. Statewide, fewer than half of Utah students met proficiency standards in any core subject. The results were reported by KPCW on Sept. 15, 2026.
